headline_marked: [[Node.js cuts major releases to one a year]] due to maintainer burnout crisis
headline: Node.js cuts major releases to one a year due to maintainer burnout crisis
summary: Node.js is shifting from two major releases to one annual Long-Term Support (LTS) version, a move driven by maintainer burnout from patching multiple active code branches. This change aims to reduce the workload on the release team.
details: Node.js is reducing its major releases from two to one per year, with every new version now becoming an LTS release. This change is primarily driven by the Node.js release team experiencing burnout from backporting security fixes across multiple live code branches. The new schedule aims to alleviate this burden.

The previous decade-old schedule involved a new Current release every April and October, with only even-numbered versions promoted to 30-month LTS. Odd-numbered releases, despite minimal real-world adoption, still required security backports for their six-month lifespan, contributing to the team's workload of managing "four or five active lines."

Under the revised model, each major version will follow three phases: a six-month Alpha (October-March) for early testing, a six-month Current (April-October) for stabilization, and then a 30-month LTS period focused solely on security fixes. Node.js 27, the first under new rules, begins Alpha in October and ships as 27.0.0 in April 2027.

For most developers who already exclusively upgrade to LTS versions, the practical impact will be minimal, primarily involving changes to version numbering. The LTS support windows will remain similar, and every release will now be designated as LTS.

The actual efficiency gain comes from eliminating the odd-numbered Current branch, which consumed volunteer hours for security backporting despite low production use. This highlights a broader maintainer capacity issue common in open-source projects, where volunteer time is a scarce resource.

The transition has not been without concerns; some contributors, like Kevin Lentin, warned that the new annual cadence could create significant two-year gaps between major versions for teams accustomed to more frequent upgrades, potentially making it harder to catch up.
caption:

headline_marked: [[Trump's AI Safety Accord]] signed by major tech firms, but it's voluntary and non-binding
headline: Trump's AI Safety Accord signed by major tech firms, but it's voluntary and non-binding
summary: Major AI companies like Google, OpenAI, and Meta signed a voluntary White House accord on super intelligence, but critics say it lacks the sweeping regulation many in the industry are asking for.
details: Executives from Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and Nvidia signed "The White House Accord on Super Intelligence" after a luncheon hosted by President Donald Trump. Trump described the effort as "tremendous self-regulation," yet the agreement falls short of the comprehensive AI regulation many within these companies have advocated for.

The voluntary commitments encourage companies to implement robust internal controls for monitoring AI capabilities and preventing unintended rogue behavior. They also suggest empowering internal teams for this work and partnering with external monitors for independent assessments. Finally, the accord recommends that company boards establish committees to oversee these safety efforts.

While these pledges signal an attempt by frontier AI labs to develop safe products for the public, any hopes for a broad government endorsement were quickly tempered. News broke that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) intends to investigate several AI companies regarding potential consumer protection issues.

This statement is the result of weeks of debate over AI regulation and follows previous voluntary agreements, such as the "Frontier AI Safety Commitments" announced by the UK and South Korea in early 2025. Notably, frontier AI labs had also sought an antitrust exemption to coordinate on safety work without regulatory scrutiny.

Neil Chilson, a former chief technologist for the FTC, noted that the commission could potentially enforce these pledges if a company materially failed to follow through. However, the typical FTC remedy for deceptive business practices is usually a promise not to lie again, rather than mandating massive reforms.

For instance, a recent FTC settlement with companies accused of misrepresenting ad targeting services based on voice recordings focused on preventing future misrepresentation. The settlement did not address the legality of collecting voice data itself or set new guardrails for such practices.
caption:
